If retention after authorization is not allowed: (1) limit CVC use to the synchronous initial authorization request, including any cascade within that request, and delete the CVC when the request completes; (2) perform incremental authorizations by referencing the original authorization, without the CVC; (3) rewrite 12.4, NFR-6, the Section 24 CVC decision and the NFR-6 test to say 'absent upon completion of authorization'.

findings.statement: Section 12.4, NFR-6 and the confirmed CVC decision store the CVC, encrypted, until settlement or for up to 72 hours. The basis given is that PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow sensitive authentication data to be kept until the transaction settles. As the reviewer understands PCI DSS, card verification codes may not be kept once authorization is complete, even in encrypted form. The incremental-authorization use case needs the CVC after the first authorization has completed, so the design keeps it past authorization by construction. If the cited reading is wrong, the CDE cannot pass the Level 1 assessment required by NFR-5. The document also cites v4.0, and whether that is the version that will be in force at assessment has not been checked.
findings.title: CVC retention until settlement relies on an unverified reading of PCI DSS

findings.statement: Section 9.3 says one partition sustains 10,000 WCU per second and that two writes per request give about 1,800 WCU for M-0001 at 900 TPS. The per-partition figure is far above the reviewer's understanding of DynamoDB's documented limit and must be checked. The WCU arithmetic also ignores item size (response_body up to 4 KB) and the extra writes from the LSI. Separately, the LSI keeps each merchant's whole item collection together, which may hit a size limit for a merchant writing millions of records a day. If any of these premises fails, idempotency throttles for the merchant carrying 45% of peak traffic, which would be an outage at expected load against NFR-1 and NFR-3. Separately, 9.1's 'after expiry is treated as new' assumes TTL deletion is immediate. If expired items persist, the attribute_not_exists put fails and the request is wrongly treated as a duplicate.
findings.title: DynamoDB capacity claims for idempotency keyed by merchant_id are unverified

Add to 20.2 a post-failover recovery procedure that rebuilds lost authorizations from acquirer status queries and settlement files, and reverses orphan holds. (b) Adopt a synchronous cross-region commit for authorization and ledger records, and re-budget the commit step in 21.1. Update the NFR-4 test to match.

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings, including loss of a whole region. Section 20.2 relies on Aurora Global Database replication, which it describes as asynchronous with lag typically under one second. Asynchronous replication cannot guarantee that commits survive an unplanned regional loss. The NFR-4 game-day criterion ('every ledger posting committed... present after failover') therefore cannot be reliably met. Authorizations lost in the lag window would leave acquirer-side holds and approvals with no internal payment record, which breaks P1.
findings.title: Zero RPO on region loss claimed over asynchronous Aurora Global Database replication

findings.statement: Section 11.2 says cascading cannot duplicate because the previous attempt did not succeed. findings.statement: Every detokenise unwraps a DEK in the HSM with no caching. findings.statement: Section 14 enforces a per-currency balance invariant at commit and writes journals in the same transaction as the state change, which avoids dual writes. It also moves balance updates off the payment path to avoid hot rows.
